"more or less continuous expositions by a speaker who wants the audience to learn something"

Bligh, What's the Use of Lectures?

common forms of lecture organization

1 hierarchic forms

a the classification hierarchy

  • "Assuming that the organization of information requires grouping in some way, this is about the simplest form there can be. Each item of information is linked with only one other idea, so that the grouping aids the memory while there are a minimum of links to be remembered."
  • "Since, for most people, there is a limit to the number of items they can remember under one heading, it is advisable to subdivide them when there are more than nine, and preferably when there are more than five."

b the problem-centered lecture

  • "In using the problem-centered form, the lecturer asks a question or presents a problem and thereafter gives information, arguments, and hypotheses as possible solutions, so that everything said focuses on the initial problem."

2 chaining

  • "A story consists of a chain of events; perhaps it is because both our experience and our speech are in sequential form that chaining seems a natural form of exposition."
  • "Assuming the links between one stage and the next are easy to follow, chaining is a form of organization that maintains attention very well, as may be evident from the use of stories with children; but if attention is lost, it is difficult for the student to pick up the thread again."
  • "the lecturer who adopts the chaining form must employ tracking devices so that students may mentally return to where they left off."

3 variations and more complex forms

a comparison

  • "A common variant of the hierarchic form is the comparison. It is a form of paired classification."

b the thesis

  • "If one regards a complex argument as the answer to a problem supported by a chain of reasoning, a lecture presenting a thesis is likely to be a combination of the chaining and problem-centered forms."

c logical dichotomy

  • "A particularly useful variation of the hierarchic form is the logical dichotomy. Its merit is that it may break down a complex subject without omissions."

d network

  • "Each facet is linked with many others to produce a complex network of interrelationships. But because a lecture necessarily takes place in time, it has a linear form."

making the organization clear

  • "It has already been suggested that summaries of a whole lecture both at the beginning and the end are often recommended."
  • "Certainly the dictum 'First tell 'em what you're gonna tell 'em; then tell 'em; and then tell 'em what you've told 'em' can usefully be applied to lectures and is particularly appropriate to those who teach a difficult subject or who cannot easily get down to the students' level of understanding."

1 introductions: state the organization at the beginning

  • "A lecture is likely to be more effective if its organization is given at the beginning."
giving framework1. Announce lecture topic.
2. Outline the structure.
3. Indicate its scope.
4. Present lecturer's aims.
setting context5. Show importance and relevance of topic.
6. Refer to earlier lectures.
7. Relate new topic to given material.
  • "Thompson made two pertinent observations. First, lecturers mix and muddle these functions. For example, mentioning 1, 4, 6, 7, 4, 3, 5 in that order was typical. It might be better to follow the order in Table 5.2."
introductions"What I'm going to talk about is . . . OK . . . All right . . . Last time . . . To begin with . . . Let us begin."
new key point"The next thing is . . . Another development was . . . As you may have heard . . . Firstly . . . You can imagine what happened . . . The problem is . . . The surprising thing is . . . (Display on blackboard or screen)"
conclusions"To sum up . . . In conclusion . . . In this lecture . . . Where does this take us? . . . How does all this answer the question with which we began? . . . Well . . . X, y and z in this lecture lead us to consider question Q next time."

table 5.1. common macro signals of lecture organization.

2 for each new point: itemize

  • "In the absence of an advance organizer, each item provides a peg on which detail may be hung. Detail is best remembered by association, and the item provides this."
  • "Although it may be obvious to lecturers whenever they are going on to a fresh point, this is not so obvious to listeners, least of all students who are not already familiar with the topic."
  • "If students daydream, or have microsleeps, they may easily lose the thread of an argument. If points are itemized, they will know they have lost a point; they might pick it up again more easily and then fill it in with the help of another student later."
  • "Itemization is an aid to memory. Revision from notes is more thorough if the students know, say, that 'there are five points to be remembered on this topic and seven on the other.'"

3 for each new point: use a visual buildup

  • "The organization of itemized points will be clearer if they are displayed on a blackboard or screen immediately after being mentioned."
  • "With most lecture forms numbering, indenting, and underlining assist clarity by differentiating points and indicating their relative importance."
  • "Students are more likely to note what is written on the board partly because they believe it must be important if the lecturer has taken the trouble, and partly because they have time to write it when the lecturer stops the steady flow of words to do the same."
  • "For these two reasons, the display is a valuable technique of emphasis."

notes on using overhead projector

  • "The organization can be progressively revealed or shown all at once."
  • "Black on white is perceived 15 percent more quickly and copied with fewer errors than white on black."
  • "Color is more pleasing against a white background and color coding can be used to contrast levels in a hierarchy."
  • "Transparencies provide both a permanent record and continuity from one lecture and the next."
  • "The overlay facility allows both buildup and breakdown of complex diagrams (as with anatomy or engine parts)."

4 for conclusions, take stock and summarize

  • "The technique of taking stock, which consists of reviewing what has been said up to that time, is valuable for setting the next point in its context. It aids learning by showing how the parts are related to the whole."

source: writings/bligh5.pdf, chapter 5, pp. 69–88.
